stops.name: Vouillé, the campus Vogladensis, Alaric slain by the king's hand
stops.campa: On the field of Vouillé, at the tenth milestone from Poitiers, the armies meet: the Goths fight from a distance with darts, the Franks press in with the sword, and the Goths flee as is their custom. Clovis wins the victory, God helping him, and kills Alaric the king with his own hand. As he strikes, two Goths come at him suddenly with lances from either side, but his cuirass and his swift horse deliver him from death. Aquitaine is won in an afternoon; Amalaric, Alaric's son, flees to Spain; the Gothic kingdom of Toulouse is finished.

stops.name: Bordeaux, the winter quarters
stops.campa: The king winters in Bordeaux, the Garonne city of the Goths now a Frankish court. From here he orders the reduction of the south: his son Theodoric is sent by way of Albi and Rodez to Clermont, and brings under his father's dominion the cities from the boundary of the Goths to the limit of the Burgundians. The map of France is being drawn this winter, road by road, in the itineraries of a nineteen-year-old prince and the garrisons of a baptized army.

stops.name: Toulouse, the treasure of Alaric
stops.campa: Clovis enters Toulouse and takes all the treasures of Alaric: the hoard of the Balt kings, gathered since the sack of Rome a century before, wagonloads of the south's gold going north under Frankish spears. The city where Syagrius was surrendered in chains twenty-one years ago now surrenders everything. The kingdom that reigned in Toulouse for ninety years is carried away in its own coffers.

stops.name: Angoulême, the walls fall of their own accord
stops.campa: The king comes to Angoulême, and the Lord gives him such grace that the walls fall down of their own accord when he gazes at them. No engines, no ladders: the city opens like Jericho before the new Joshua. He drives out the Goths and takes the town under his own dominion, and with this the victory is complete. He turns north for Tours, bringing many gifts for the holy church of the blessed Martin, whose goodwill he guarded with an edict and whose psalm girded him for the battle.

stops.name: Tours, Saint Martin's, consul and Augustus
stops.campa: Letters come from the emperor Anastasius at Constantinople conferring the consulship. In the church of the blessed Martin the king clothes himself in the purple tunic and the chlamys and sets a diadem on his head; then he mounts his horse and rides from the gate of Saint Martin's atrium to the cathedral, scattering gold and silver among the people with his own hand along the whole way. From that day he is called consul or Augustus. The barbarian king wears Rome's colors in Martin's own house: the old empire hands its western title to the new France.

stops.name: Paris, the seat of the kingdom
stops.campa: Leaving Tours he goes to Paris, and there he establishes the seat of his kingdom: the island city of the Parisii in its river, Geneviève's city; the shepherdess who turned Attila aside still lives within its walls to see the Frank make it a capital. Theodoric his son comes to him there. From this decision the whole shape of France descends: whatever the kingdom will be, it will be governed from this island, and the kings of a thousand years will reign where Clovis set his chair.

stops.name: Cologne, Sigibert, Chloderic, and the treasure chest
stops.campa: From Paris, Clovis sends secretly to the son of Sigibert the Lame: your father is old and limps on his weak foot; if he should die, his kingdom and our friendship would come to you. Chloderic has his father murdered as he sleeps at midday in the forest of Buchaw, and Clovis' envoys, come to view the dead king's treasure, bid him plunge his hand to the bottom of the chest. As he bends far over, an axe splits his skull. Then Clovis comes to Cologne, spreads his hands in innocence before the people, and they raise him on the shield and make him king.
stops.quote: I cannot shed the blood of my own kinsmen, which it is a crime to do. But since this has happened, I give you my advice, if it seems acceptable; turn to me, that you may be under my protection.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.40 (trans. Brehaut), Clovis to the people of Cologne

stops.name: Thérouanne, Chararic tonsured and slain (traditional seat)
stops.campa: Now he turns to Chararic, who at Soissons stood at a distance waiting to befriend the victor. Clovis entraps him with his son, imprisons them, and has them tonsured, the shears through the royal hair are a deposition deeper than death, ordaining the father priest and the son deacon. Chararic weeps at his degradation, and his son speaks the words that doom them: green wood sprouts. Word comes to Clovis that they mean to let their hair grow and kill him, and he orders both put to death, and takes their kingdom with the treasures and people.
stops.quote: It was on green wood that these twigs were cut, and they are not altogether withered. They will shoot out quickly, and be able to grow; may he perish as swiftly who has done this.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.41 (trans. Brehaut), the son of Chararic

stops.name: Cambrai, Ragnachar, Ricchar, and the false gold
stops.campa: Ragnachar of Cambrai, unbridled in everything, his vile counselor Farro at his ear, is sold before the battle begins: Clovis has bought his leudes with arm-bands and sword-belts of gold: gilded bronze, false to the core. Beaten in the field, Ragnachar is seized by his own men and brought bound before Clovis with his brother Ricchar. The king reproaches him for disgracing their blood by suffering bonds, and the axe falls; to Ricchar: had you aided your brother, he would not have been bound, and the axe again. The betrayers discover their gold is counterfeit; such gold, says the king, as traitors deserve.
stops.quote: Why have you humiliated our family in permitting yourself to be bound? It would have been better for you to die.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.42 (trans. Brehaut)

stops.name: Paris, the lament that is a trap
stops.campa: Having killed many other kings and his nearest relatives, jealous lest they take the kingdom from him, he has extended his rule over all the Gauls. Now he gathers his people together and mourns aloud the kinsmen he himself destroyed, a stranger among foreigners with no kin to help him in adversity. But he says this not from grief, Gregory records, but as a ruse: if perchance some relative still lives, the lament may draw him out of hiding to be killed. None comes. The chronicler writes down the cunning without blinking, and adds that God was laying the king's enemies low because he walked with an upright heart.
stops.quote: Woe to me, who have remained as a stranger among foreigners, and have none of my kinsmen to give me aid if adversity comes.
stops.quote_source: Gregory of Tours, Historia Francorum II.42 (trans. Brehaut)

stops.name: Orléans, the first council of the Frankish church
stops.campa: By order of the king, thirty-two bishops of Gaul assemble at Orléans, five metropolitans among them, Cyprian of Bordeaux presiding, the bishops of the conquered Gothic south sitting beside those of the old Frankish north for the first time under one crown. They pass thirty-one canons on sanctuary, on church property, on the ordination of clerics, and send their decrees to the absent king for his confirmation, addressing him as the son of the catholic Church. The alliance of throne and altar that will carry France to 1789 is drafted here, in one July session, four months before the king dies.
stops.quote: To their lord, the son of the catholic Church, the most glorious king Clovis: all the bishops whom you have commanded to come to the council.
stops.quote_source: Acta of the First Council of Orléans (511), salutation of the synodal letter (MGH Concilia I)

stops.name: Paris, the death of the king
stops.campa: After all this he dies at Paris, in the fifth year after the battle of Vouillé. All the days of his reign are thirty years, and his age is forty-five. Gregory sets the mark of the saint on the span of the king: from the death of Saint Martin to the death of King Clovis, in the eleventh year of the episcopate of Licinius of Tours, one hundred and twelve years are reckoned: the history of Gaul measured from confessor to convert. The kingdom is divided among his four sons, Theodoric, Chlodomer, Childebert and Chlothar, and the story of France begins its long argument among heirs.
